topics.topic: Backup encryption format, authentication, key representation, and key-digest construction
questions: Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, key encoding or derivation, nonce generation and file authentication rules define an encrypted backup and detect a wrong key or modified ciphertext?
Which digest algorithm and byte representation produce the recorded key digest, and is it an unkeyed fingerprint or another identifier?
Which authenticated-encryption algorithm, nonce construction, key representation and key-digest algorithm are used, and is the readable metadata authenticated with the encrypted payload?
Which authenticated-encryption format, algorithm, nonce generation, key derivation and key-digest algorithm define an encrypted backup and detect ciphertext or metadata tampering?

quotes: Each backup is encrypted with the backup key the configuration holds at its making (A17).
A backup cannot be read without the key it was made with.
judgement.why: This is the same backup-encryption construction, key interpretation, metadata-authentication and key-digest question already assigned to State 6.

questions: Which cookie attributes, host/domain, path and SameSite policy make "Registry's own origin" exact, given that browser cookies are not scoped by port and therefore not strictly by origin?

What exact cookie attributes and transport rule implement this, especially for an interface reached locally without HTTPS, given that cookies are scoped by host and path rather than by origin or port?
What exact cookie scope and attributes implement “only to Registry's own origin,” given that browser cookies are scoped by host/domain and path rather than by origin or port?

   to Registry's own origin.
judgement.why: This is the same owner-session cookie attributes, scope, transport and deletion-policy question already assigned to State 6.

What makes each location, credential, token and backup key well formed, including the character encoding used to measure a secret's 32-byte minimum and compare secret equality?

topics.topic: Owner-interface behavior when no backup has readable metadata
questions: What does the owner interface show or return when no kept backup exists, or when files under the kept prefix exist but none has readable metadata?
What does the owner interface show when the newest prefixed file has unreadable metadata, or when no readable kept backup exists?
Before a backup run deletes it, what does the owner interface do when a kept-prefix file has unreadable metadata: ignore it, refuse the view, or report that backup state is invalid?

quotes:
The owner interface shows the instant of the newest kept backup, read from the
   kept backups.

Third, whatever the second step did, it deletes every kept
   backup made more than 30 × 24 hours before, and every file under the kept
   prefix whose unencrypted record (rule 1) cannot be read. It takes the
   files in the order of their names; a file it cannot read or delete is
   reported, and it goes on with the next.
judgement.divergence: One implementation ignores unreadable kept-prefix files and shows the newest readable backup or no backup, while another refuses the owner-interface view or reports an invalid backup state; the owner notices the different interface result.
judgement.why: The texts require a newest-backup display and describe unreadable files, but do not define the display when no readable kept-backup metadata exists.

topics.topic: Serialization of successful imports with concurrent activity in other owner sessions
questions: How is accepting an import serialized with uploads in other owner sessions so that an upload which passed the closure check before the import committed cannot finish afterward and leave a file retained despite the closure?

How is a successful confirmation ordered against an upload in a different owner session, so that an upload which passed its closure check cannot install a file after the successful import has performed the cross-session drop?

How are an accepted import and concurrent uploads, mapping displays or confirmations in other owner sessions ordered so that no upload can be stored after the closure check but after the successful import has dropped all files?

quotes:
The requests of one owner session that change its state — showing a
   confirmation step, uploading a file, a submission, a sign-out — are
   applied one at a time, in the order in which they take the session's one
   lock, after passing the session check: each sees the
   session as the one before left it, and other requests are not held by
   them, so a confirmation
   bound to a file a later upload replaced is refused (A16 rule 2).

An accepted import drops the
   uploaded file of every owner session (M11); a confirmation shown in
   another session is refused because the import is closed (rule 8).

Confirmations are applied
   one at a time: of two concurrent ones, the second finds the closure and is
   refused (rule 8).

While the closure exists, uploading and confirming an import are refused
   (R0-79).
judgement.divergence: One implementation serializes uploads across sessions with import acceptance so no upload can remain after closure, while another checks closure before an upload and lets that upload install its file after the successful import's cross-session drop; owners in the latter session notice whether the file and mapping remain.
judgement.why: Per-session locking and confirmation serialization do not specify the ordering of a successful import against an already-admitted upload in another owner session.

topics.topic: Whether an admitted request must revalidate the session after concurrent sign-out
questions: If a request passes the session check before sign-out but takes the session lock after sign-out has ended and removed the session, must it still run, or must it observe the ended session and be refused?

If request A passes the session check, sign-out then takes the session lock first, and A takes it afterward, does A still run, may it change session state, or is it refused because the session has ended?

If a request passes the session check but is waiting for the session lock when sign-out takes the lock first, does that already-admitted request still execute, or is session validity checked again after the lock is acquired?

quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.
judgement.why: This is the same question already answered: a request admitted before sign-out completes its store change even if it acquires the session lock later.

precedent.topic: Effect of sign-out on previously admitted concurrent requests
quotes:
A sign-out is applied in turn with the session's other requests that
   change it: one admitted before it completes its change to the store, and
   leaves nothing in the ended session.
precedent.why: A request admitted before sign-out completes its store change even if it acquires the session lock later, while no state remains in the ended session.

topics.topic: At-most-once daily backup scheduling across restarts and clock changes
questions: What happens when Registry starts or restarts exactly at 03:00, or the system clock repeats or jumps across 03:00: how is at most one run for a UTC date determined without making up a missed run?
How is at-most-once execution for a UTC day enforced across a restart at 03:00, a backward clock correction, or a process that observes 03:00 more than once, and is that due-state durable?

quotes:
These runs are R0-89's daily backups: one is due each day, and the days
   this rule and rule 5 leave without a kept backup are allowed. Every day at
   03:00 UTC, while Registry runs with its service tokens, it
   makes one backup run; a 03:00 that finds Registry stopped, or in an
   owner-only start (rule 9), makes no run, and none is made later in its
   place. Runs never overlap: a 03:00 that finds a run still going makes no
   run of its own.

The owner interface shows the instant of the newest kept backup, read from the
   kept backups.
judgement.divergence: One implementation durably records the UTC date and prevents a second run after a restart or backward clock change, while another schedules from process-local clock observations and may make two backups for that date; the owner notices different kept backups, newest-backup instants and storage use.
judgement.why: The texts specify the nominal time and prohibit overlapping runs but do not define at-most-once scheduling across restarts or repeated clock observations.

topics.topic: Backup audit sequence value for a store with no audit entries
questions: What value is recorded and what does the check require for a new store whose audit log has no entries?
What sequence value is recorded and checked when the store has never written an audit entry?

quotes:
It
   records, readable without its key, its instant, the release that made it,
   the last audit sequence number it holds and a digest of the key it was
   made with (never the key); its age is counted from that instant.

Second, it
   writes the backup under a temporary name and checks it: it decrypts it
   into a second temporary file, opens that for reading only, checks that it
   is the store version of its release, that the store's own integrity check
   passes and that its audit log ends at the recorded sequence number, and
   removes it; a backup that passes is renamed to its kept name, one that
   fails is deleted.
judgement.why: This is the same empty-audit-log sequence representation and validation question already assigned to State 6.

topics.topic: File-retention rule for confirmations refused after another session accepts an import
questions: When one session accepts the import and thereby drops another session's file, does the other session's subsequently refused confirmation keep its file as the first sentence requires, or remain without it as the changed rule requires?
Does a confirmation refused because another session already accepted the import keep its session's uploaded file, or is that refusal an exception because the successful import already dropped it?

quotes:
A refused
   confirmation keeps it, and the step may be shown again;

An accepted import drops the
   uploaded file of every owner session (M11); a confirmation shown in
   another session is refused because the import is closed (rule 8).
judgement.why: The accepted import has already dropped every session's file, so the later refused confirmation preserves the resulting absence rather than recreating the dropped file.

topics.topic: Precedence and ordering of missing-variable and unknown-variable configuration failures
questions: When required variables are missing while one or more unknown `REGISTRY_` variables are also present, which failure is first, and where do unknown variables fall in the declared item order?
When missing and unknown variables coexist, or several unknown REGISTRY_ variables exist, which failure is first, since unknown variables have no position in rule 1's item order?

quotes:
The checks run in one
   order and the first that fails stops the start: every item of rule 1
   present and none unknown; each well formed; each secret's length (rule 3);
   their distinctness (rule 4); the store and backup location apart (rule
   5); the backup location writable, by a probe file under the temporary
   prefix (A18 rule 5); the store opening, or made new (rule 5).

Within one
   check, items go in the order rule 1 lists them.
judgement.divergence: One implementation reports the first missing listed item before considering unknown variables, while another reports an unknown variable first and may choose different unknowns by environment iteration order; the owner notices a different first startup diagnostic.
judgement.why: Unknown variables have no position in rule 1's item order, so the required first-failure behavior is not determined when missing and unknown variables coexist.

quotes:
These runs are R0-89's daily backups: one is due each day, and the days

A tested restore exists every day
judgement.why: The normative rule permits days without a kept backup, while the consequence says a tested restore exists every day.
